newsitem.title: JAPAN: DKB says checking details of more improper loans.
newsitem.headline: DKB says checking details of more improper loans.

text.p: Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd (DKB) is currently investigating the details of some improper loans it has made which are not related to the Nomura Securities Co Ltd racketeer scandal, DKB president Katsuhiko Kondo said on Wednesday.
He told a parliamentary committee that the amount of such improper loans was small, but added: "We will fully investigate these."

Miyazaki told the same committee that he had not met the racketeer Koike or his younger brother, but said that he and DKB's former top executives had close contact with a "former publishing company president" who had introduced Koike to DKB.
Miyazaki said that the now-deceased former publishing company president had been a corporate racketeer but quit this business in the 1960s.
"He was an important client at our bank's branch," Miyazaki said.
Miyazaki added that he had attended the marriage ceremony of the son of the former publisher. "I had contact with him openly... I have never been asked by him to do something," he said.
Kondo said that the bank had set aside loan-loss provisions of 7.5 billion yen on loans to the Koike group, but would keep trying to recover the loans.

Asked why DKB did not until recently sell shares in Nomura which the Koike group put up as collateral for a part of the DKB loans, even though the loans became non-performing, Kondo said Nomura's share price had been too low to sell at the time.
Japanese media have reported that DKB loans provided in 1989 were used to help the racketeer group buy 300,000 Nomura shares and the group put up these shares as collateral for the loans.
According to the reports, the racketeer was able to put pressure on Nomura to give him preferential treatment as he was a major Nomura shareholder.

On May 13, Japan's securities watchdog filed a criminal complaint with prosecutors against Nomura, two former Nomura executives and an official currently with the firm, alleging they compensated a client linked to a racketeer for investment losses. The complaint came after Nomura announced irregular stock deals on March 6.
Since then, prosecutors have arrested the two former executives and the official still with the firm as well as corporate racketeer Ryuichi Koike and his younger brother, Yoshinori Koike.
Prosecutors raided DKB last Tuesday in connection with the Nomura scandal.
